item.title: Harry and Meghan See Their California Dreams — and Riches — Fade Away
item.description:
It began with such high hopes.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex landed in Hollywood in 2020, flush with a multimillion-dollar Netflix deal and a promise that the duo, scorned by the royal family, would make a slew of inspirational programming.

Two years later, “Harry & Meghan” the Netflix six-part docuseries on the couple’s departure from Britain, generated 23.4 million views in its initial release, immediately topping the company’s charts as the most watched ever for the first four days of a documentary. In total, the program has garnered 70 million views since its debut.

Nothing else Prince Harry and his wife, Meghan, ever made for the service — whether it was “Live to Lead,” a seven-episode interview show with world leaders, or “Polo,” a docuseries about the sport — reached such heights.

In 2025, the Netflix deal was not renewed. A similarly lofty agreement at Spotify also fell short of expectations.

And as Americans asked this week why the couple was leaving their West Coast idyll, Hollywood observers pointed to one of the most enduring themes in the history of Southern California: show business aspirations that failed.

“There has always been this aura here, this magical thinking,” said Leo Braudy, a Los Angeles cultural historian and the author of “The Frenzy of Renown: Fame and Its History.” “Everybody thinks, ‘I’m beautiful,’ or ‘I’m handsome.’ Everybody thinks, ‘If those people can make it in Hollywood, so can I.’”

But most people don’t make it, he said, and throughout history, even otherwise wealthy and powerful people have mistakenly imagined that success in other fields would automatically translate to show business glory.

“If there was an easy path to success in show business,” Mr. Braudy said, “there would be a lot fewer flops in Hollywood.”

The Duke and Duchess made waves this week on both sides of the Atlantic after people familiar with the decision confirmed that they were returning to England.

Six years ago, the couple, after clashing with the royal family, had exiled themselves to California, where the duchess had grown up and once had an acting career in Los Angeles.

Settling into a sprawling estate in the wealthy enclave of Montecito, Calif., the couple raised two children, Archie, 7, and Lilibet, 5.

But they now have enrolled their children in school in Britain and timed the move to coincide with the start of classes next month, according to sources who spoke to The New York Times.

It is unclear whether they will launch new business ventures or where they will live in Britain. (They were told to vacate their official residence on the grounds of Windsor Castle in 2023, the couple’s press secretary said at the time.)

A representative for the couple on Friday framed their departure from California as a short-term move.

“On the heels of a wonderful trip with family and friends this summer, Harry and Meghan have decided to spend an extended period in the U.K. this autumn,” the representative said in a statement. “They are excited to have their children spend more time in the country that’s such an important part of their family’s story.”

The royal couple’s fortunes began contracting when Netflix did not renew their overall deal last year.

In its place, the streaming giant established a much less generous pact, which still exists, whereby they would be paid only if they produced a show or a film Netflix was interested in airing. (The streaming giant still pays for office space at Raleigh Studios in Hollywood for the couple’s company, Archewell Productions.)

Separately, Netflix constructed a joint business deal with Meghan for “As Ever,” her nascent lifestyle brand which drafted off her television show, “With Love, Meghan.” An accompanying endeavor would sell products like a $28 orange blossom honey and a $14 apricot spread.

Netflix manufactured those products through its consumer product group in a revenue-sharing deal.

But the show didn’t perform up to Netflix’s standards: The first season attracted 6.1 million views, the second season earned 2.3 million views and the Christmas special had 2.6 million views.

Netflix decided to not greenlight any new seasons and ended the brand endeavor in March. Now all consumer goods are handled by Meghan’s own company. (The $12 blackberry jam is still available on the website.)

The duo’s foray into podcasts didn’t go as planned, either.

In 2020, they signed a $20 million deal with Spotify. But they only produced one season of “Archetypes,” in which Meghan hosted and interviewed guests such as Serena Williams and Paris Hilton.

Harry never made anything, despite workshopping ideas with the company for a year. (One idea, said one person close to the couple, was taste-testing hot chocolate around the country.)

It is unclear whether they were paid the full amount of the three-year deal, considering they only made one 12-episode season. A representative for the couple declined to comment. Spotify also declined to comment.

In 2023, Jeremy Zimmer, then the head of United Talent Agency, sat for an interview at the Cannes Lion marketing festival with Semafor, a digital news site, just one week after the Spotify deal fizzled and defined the problem: “Turns out Meghan Markle was not a great audio talent, or necessarily any kind of talent. And, you know, just because you’re famous doesn’t make you great at something.”

Bill Simmons, a Spotify executive and prominent podcaster, was more blunt. He called the couple “grifters,” using an expletive, in a 2023 podcast after the Spotify deal fell apart.

Meghan’s most recent project, “Cookie Queens,” a documentary about the Girl Scouts and their cookie sale ambitions that she executive produced, was not a huge hit at the box office. (“CatVideoFest 2026,” a film that compiled the best cat videos on the internet, out grossed hers.)

Yet, according to Howard Cohen, the distributor of the movie through his Roadside Attractions company, the movie will ultimately be a success.

Released on only 446 screens, the film is nearing $1 million at the box office and will be available to rent through streaming on Sept. 8. With documentaries struggling in theaters, the movie is, in fact, the highest-grossing noncelebrity documentary to be released so far this year.

Meghan’s appearance at both Sundance, where it initially debuted, and at screenings in Los Angeles and Ojai helped buoy those numbers, Mr. Cohen said in an interview.

Meghan will also appear in the Amazon Prime movie “Close Personal Friends” that is set to be released on the streaming service next spring. The film stars Brie Larsen and Lily Collins and is set in Santa Barbara. Meghan plays herself in a cameo.

The duchess is also in early talks to appear in the third season of the Netflix crime series “The Gentlemen.” Should the deal come to fruition, Meghan would film the role in Britain. (The second season has yet to air and Netflix has yet to greenlight a third.)

At least one Hollywood veteran was upbeat about their return to Britain.

“My first thought was, smart play!” said Spencer Pratt, the reality television star who ran unsuccessfully for Los Angeles mayor this year. “Show business in the U.K. is booming, unlike here.”

He said his wife, Heidi Montag, a reality television star who was a fan of Meghan’s lifestyle show, “got all emotional” this week at the possibility that Prince Harry might be reconciling with the royal family.

In Britain, he said, the couple could take advantage of local tax breaks for film and television production, which are more generous than those in California, and use their own “palaces and castles” as backdrops.

“From a business perspective, I think they have more potential to make content for Netflix or Paramount Plus or whoever from England,” he added. “I personally would already watch a season of, like, ‘With Love, Meghan and Harry: Back to the Pond.’”

How the couple’s new life in Britain will affect their show business prospects is uncertain. Like many whose Hollywood dreams fall short, Harry and Meghan are moving away but have not ruled out a return.

A representative of Harry and Meghan said the couple’s businesses are continuing unchanged. And they will still have a toehold in the U.S., as they are keeping their historic $14.5 million home in Montecito.

item.title: For Some in a Disrupted D.C., Grand Prix Is More Irritation Than Celebration
item.description:
Downtown traffic has snarled, as crews scurry to put up barriers, weld down manhole covers and even relocate traffic lights.

The National Gallery of Art has conducted vibration studies and put up protective panels around some of its outdoor sculptures, while other nearby Smithsonian museums prepared to reduce public access.

Airlines have rerouted flights, as the closest airport braces for a temporary shutdown. And at least one school within the exclusion zone has had to go fully remote.

Even before the first engine has revved in Washington’s first Grand Prix this weekend, the effects of turning a warren of museums and historic landmarks at the seat of government into a 1.7-mile IndyCar racecourse have rippled across the capital. And for some residents and commuters, the resulting disruptions are wearing thin in a summer that has been full of them.

“It’s putting additional stress on a stressful situation,” Jason Cummins, who commutes regularly from Baltimore to Washington, said on Friday as he walked near the race perimeter back to his parked car. His drive into the city, normally about an hour, had taken twice as long that morning, he said.

“I understand that this is the nation’s capital,” he said, “but there’s a lot of things that happen here.”

The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is the final major event in downtown Washington to mark the United States’ 250th anniversary, punctuating a summer that also featured a state fair exhibition, an Ultimate Fighting Championship match and a marathon Independence Day parade, concert and fireworks display. Many of those events also involved military flyovers, making them sonically inescapable for nearby residents.

And all of them have been heavily promoted by President Trump, in a city already wary of his attempts to leave his imprint on it.

For the race, Trump administration has planned a two-day extravaganza, complete with more flyovers, fireworks and an honorary presidential lap of the course. The main event will feature 25 drivers zipping around for 147 laps, crisscrossing the National Mall and making tight turns around some of the nation’s most iconic buildings.

Race organizers have handed out about 140,000 tickets to spectators, which is also being broadcast on Fox Sports. And Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, has recorded a number of promotional videos to hype the event, repeating what has become its patriotic catchphrase: “Freedom doesn’t ring — it revs.”

While the race is expected to draw crowds, it is also expected to hamper other activities in and around the city, such as the National Book Festival, which is taking place a few blocks north of the race perimeter on Saturday, and travel in and out of Ronald Reagan National Airport, which announced a three-hour shutdown to coincide with the prerace festivities on Sunday.

Yet organizers, federal officials and the city’s mayor, Muriel Bowser, have said they would be open to the race becoming a tradition.

“It’s not just fun and games for our city. These are events that draw tens of thousands of people to our city,” the mayor’s office said in a statement. “Those visitors stay in our hotels, go to our restaurants, they visit our neighborhoods. For D.C., that means more good-paying jobs and more opportunity for our workers and businesses.”

Representatives of the race organizers did not respond to a request for comment.

A day before the race festivities were set to begin, the streets around downtown Washington were eerily quiet, even for a summer Friday. Residents and commuters, it appeared, had heeded city leaders’ exhortations to use the Metro, or simply stay home.

But for those whom public transportation was not a viable option, the many street closures, which extended for blocks beyond the racecourse itself, had given the city a labyrinthine feel.

“I was down there, and I thought, I’m never going to get an Uber here,” said Richelle Smith, walking away from the race perimeter to find a ride home to Chevy Chase, a nearby Maryland suburb. “I’m trying to walk to where I can even catch one.”

“Why they doing a race downtown, I don’t even know,” one driver of a blue S.U.V. fumed audibly through rolled-down windows, as he pulled up to a stoplight on the edge of the race perimeter, and made a sharp right turn to detour.

Staging an IndyCar race in a city does not mean just throwing up barricades. City streets must also be turned into flat track. That means manhole covers must be shaved down, or built up with special epoxy until they are level with the street, and welded shut, so they do not turn into inadvertent projectiles as cars pass over them at speeds upward of 180 miles per hour.

More than 200 manhole covers were welded down along the course, Doug Boles, the IndyCar president, said during an interview on Newsmax this week, in which he also noted that several traffic lights had been removed.

A spokesman for the transportation department said that IndyCar was covering the cost of all such preparations, and that the Trump administration would work with city leaders to address any post-race impacts to the roads.

Washington also presents a denser urban environment than some other host cities for racecars to navigate. The course snakes around buildings, in places forcing drivers to make quick, successive turns at high speeds, and raising the risk of collisions.

“It’s going to be hard to pass here,” Mr. Boles said in the interview, noting that five of the course’s seven turns were at right angles. “Could be a little bit of carnage in this place.”

But while the promise of collisions may be part of the allure for some racing fans, they have only heightened the concerns of critics.

“For an event of this magnitude in such a symbolic, densely packed area in terms of historic sites and rare collections, an undertaking like this should not have been rushed,” Mary Okin, the assistant director of Living New Deal, a group dedicated to documenting and preserving public works projects from around the time of the Great Depression, said in an interview.

Last month, Ms. Okin sent a letter to the National Park Service, asking officials to take steps to protect the murals in Wilbur J. Cohen Federal Building, which sits on Independence Avenue along the racecourse, from potential damage. She suggested that the federal government monitor the murals, install temporary sound barriers and conduct pre- and post-race damage assessments.

But the Park Service informed her that “vibration monitoring is beyond the role of the N.P.S. for this event,” directing her to address concerns to the people responsible for managing the individual structures.

Representatives for the Park Service, as well as several museums and government buildings along the route, did not respond to requests for comment.

Across the National Mall from the Cohen building, vibration studies were carried out at the National Gallery of Art, said Chris Abanavas, a spokesman for the museum, who added that it had put in place “measures to ensure the safety of our staff, visitors, collection and facilities during the race.”

While Mr. Abanavas did not specify the measures, plywood structures were seen earlier this week around some of the outdoor sculptures and features, darkening I.M. Pei’s glass atrium skylight that erupts onto the museum’s grounds.

item.title: Judge Denies New Trial for Karmelo Anthony in Texas Teen’s Killing
item.description:
A Black teenager who was convicted of murder in the fatal stabbing of a white peer at a high school track meet last year will not receive a new trial, a Texas judge ruled on Saturday.

The teenager, Karmelo Anthony, 19, was sentenced in June after an eight-day trial centering on an altercation at a track meet in April 2025, in Frisco, Texas, a Dallas suburb, during which Mr. Anthony stabbed Austin Metcalf. Mr. Anthony and Mr. Metcalf were both 17 at the time.

Mr. Anthony was sentenced to 35 years in prison. The murder trial and sentencing inflamed racial tensions in Collin County, a predominantly white region of North Texas, and drew protesters outside the courthouse. Some called for justice for Mr. Metcalf, while others called for Mr. Anthony’s freedom.

After the sentencing, Mr. Anthony secured a new legal team to appeal his murder conviction and sentence. After hearing testimony on Thursday and Friday, a new judge in the case denied Mr. Anthony’s request for a new trial. Mr. Anthony’s lawyers had appealed the decision, which will now move to the Fifth Court of Appeals in Dallas.

Greg Willis, the Collin County district attorney, said in a statement that he had expected the court’s decision.

“The jury’s guilty verdict stands, and we remain confident in the process,” Mr. Willis said. “Every defendant has the right to appeal, and our thoughts and prayers remain with the Metcalf family in the painful wake of last week’s hearing.”

Lawyers for Mr. Anthony said in a statement that they would continue to explore legal remedies.

“This denial does not end our work,” Mr. Anthony’s legal team said. “We knew when we entered this case that this case might not be won in a single courtroom or with a single motion. We will keep advocating for Karmelo until the justice we seek is obtained.”

In June, Mr. Anthony secured a new team of lawyers, who were working pro bono. His new legal team claimed that limited access to the courtroom had violated Mr. Anthony’s right to a public trial, that the court had improperly instructed the jury and that prosecutors had prevented Mr. Anthony from testifying that he had acted in self-defense. (Mr. Anthony has not denied that he stabbed Mr. Metcalf.)

His lawyers also made a successful bid to recuse the original judge on the case, John Roach, from additional proceedings after he gave an interview to a local news outlet in which he expressed personal opinions about the jury’s verdict.

Judge Michael Chitty, who took over the case, heard from prosecutors and Mr. Anthony’s new legal team this week. Some of the testimony focused on an informal, so-called gentlemen’s agreement between prosecutors and Mr. Anthony’s original legal team in which they had decided to limit what they would share in court about Mr. Anthony’s and Mr. Metcalf’s character and past behavior.

Prosecutors had suggested an agreement in which “both sides try the case without character, reputation, or extraneous evidence” for either teenager, Mike Howard, who was one of Mr. Anthony’s lawyers, said in an affidavit.

But Mr. Anthony’s new lawyers argued that such an agreement had been too limiting during the trial, impeding Mr. Anthony’s defense.

For instance, prosecutors felt that the defense had violated the agreement by mentioning that Mr. Anthony had been involved in a chess club, according to the testimony of one of Mr. Anthony’s original lawyers, Toby Shook.

Mr. Howard said in the affidavit that prosecutors had said that “if we called Mr. Anthony to testify, character, reputation, and extraneous evidence pertaining to Mr. Anthony were in play.” Mr. Anthony then chose not to testify during the trial.

Testimony on Friday from Bill Wirskye, a prosecutor, shifted away from the agreement and focused on security concerns during the murder trial, such as death threats made against lawyers and others involved in the case.

Mr. Wirskye also said that some social media influencers and content creators had been “bad actors” in the case, spreading misinformation to attract views and clicks.

item.title: ‘It’s Been Terrible’: Thousands in Indiana Remain Without Power
item.description:
It was Day 11 without power in Gary, Ind., and Pierre Ervin was beyond fed up.

He could not eat breakfast in his dark, storm-damaged home because he had thrown out all the food rotting in his refrigerator. So he headed to work hungry on Saturday, threading his way past the snapped trees and downed power lines littering the industrial city as frustration grew with the agonizingly slow process of restoring power.

“It’s been terrible,” Mr. Ervin, 46, said.

About 30,000 customers across northern Indiana were still without electricity on Saturday evening, nearly two weeks after thunderstorms flooded neighborhoods and pummeled the region with hurricane-force winds.

About 56 percent of those people are in Gary, a majority-Black city of 67,000 that has long grappled with poverty, population loss and disinvestment as its steel industry shrank and homes and buildings were abandoned.

“My people are being overlooked,” said Myles Tolliver, a Gary councilman whose family has been staying outside Chicago while they wait for power to be restored. “Our families are sitting in the dark. We don’t need any more excuses. We need the lights on.”

On Saturday, as power returned to some customers across northern Indiana, Gary residents said they were angry and despondent to find themselves, once again, at the back of the line. The local utility, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co., said that Gary and the nearby city of Portage would be the last to have their electricity back, potentially by the end of Tuesday.

As they sat inside their dark living rooms or on porches to escape the stagnant air inside, some residents said they doubted a rich, white town would have been left to languish for so long without power.

“I don’t understand it,” said Daymond Willis, 45, a chef at a casino restaurant, who has been without power since Aug. 11. “It shouldn’t be this long. I think If we weren’t a Black city things would be different.”

On Saturday, some residents said a few businesses and apartments had gotten their power back, and more utility trucks were rolling through the streets. Steve Segura, a city spokesman, said the utility was sending an additional 85 line workers and 240 vegetation management crews.

But residents and politicians were increasingly exasperated.

Gov. Mike Braun of Indiana urged the utility to “match the urgency” of the people who had languished without power for nearly two weeks. Mr. Braun said on Friday that he requested an expedited major disaster declaration from the Federal Emergency Management Agency to bring in more resources.

“Bring in more crews,” Mr. Braun, a Republican, told the utility in a pointed social media post on Saturday. “Put every available resource into the field. Get creative. Get the job done.”

Northern Indiana Public Service Co. said its electric system had suffered “unprecedented and widespread damage” from the storm, and did not answer its 24-hour hotline for media inquiries on Saturday. An automated message said the voice mailbox was full.

On Aug. 11, Gary was pummeled by a derecho, a group of intense thunderstorms that last several hours, which brought heavy rain and damaging wind gusts of 99 miles per hour as part of a punishing parade of storms through Indiana since the start of spring. Through July, 89 tornadoes have touched down in the state this year, well above the annual average of 28, according to the National Weather Service.

“This has been a hyperactive season for us,” said Ricky Castro, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in Romeoville, Ill., southwest of Chicago.

But there was some relief in the forecast, with a very small chance of thunderstorms in Gary on Saturday and drier weather expected in coming days.

Donations and supplies of food, tarps, bottled water and repair kits have flowed into Gary, and President Trump granted an emergency declaration last week. There has been no visible presence of federal-emergency-management officials on the ground, and FEMA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Meantime, residents have come together to try to help one another through the blackout.

Some have held sidewalk barbecues to feed their neighbors. Others with generators have opened their homes to let neighbors do laundry or charge their phones.

On Saturday, more than 200 people at the CityLife community center received a lunch of fried chicken, coleslaw, potato salad and biscuits that were donated by the singer Deniece Williams, a Gary native. About a mile away, a few hundred people lined outside a strip mall up for meals donated by two Chicago-based restaurants.

Ahmed Musleh, a manager of the Save More grocery store, said the market had given away 20 cases of water and grilled hot dogs for residents in need in its parking lot, about 500 feet away from where another community group had set up to feed residents.

Mr. Musleh said his store would be able to make an insurance claim for the food it was forced to discard, but he worried that his customers on food stamps would not receive the same help.

“They were already struggling, and for them to lose an entire month of food is a big thing,” he said.

Residents said the storm had already cost their families thousands of dollars in spoiled food, lost wages, hotel bills, fuel for generators and other costs of enduring the blackout.

Keya Reed, a 51-year-old warehouse worker, and her husband, Derrick Reed, a 57-year-old maintenance worker, said they had already spent $7,000 on a generator, gasoline and a tree-cutting service to haul away a tree that had downed power lines and damaged their modest home. Even as their costs pile up, they have refused to go to food pantries or take donated foods because, they said, others in Gary need it more.

Ms. Reed, who has lived in Gary her whole life, said she and others were used to dealing with the hardship.

“Everything is always against Gary,” she said on Saturday inside her home, its air dark and stuffy, the hallways tangled with electrical lines snaking to the generator. “It’s really sad to say, but I’m used to it.”

item.title: Violent Extremist Who Targeted Young People Online Is Sentenced to 77 Years
item.description:
A federal judge in Tennessee on Wednesday sentenced a follower of violent online extremist groups to 77 years in prison after he coerced 30 young people to send him nude images, abuse animals or engage in self-mutilation, prosecutors said.

The man, Kyle William Spitze, 27, operated under the groups known as Harm Nation and 764, prosecutors said. The three digits originate from the ZIP code of the group’s founder living in Texas, according to the Anti-Defamation League.

The groups are online networks that the U.S. Department of Justice has described as part of nihilistic violent extremism, a movement sowing chaos to usher society’s downfall.

They achieve their aims, in part, by glorifying mass murder and urging victims to engage in self-harm, the authorities said.

Mr. Spitze received the “longest federal sentence ever imposed on a nihilistic violent extremist,” John A. Eisenberg, the assistant attorney general for national security for the Justice Department, said in a statement.

The sentence “sends a strong message that civil society will not tolerate such depravity,” he added.

Jonathan Cooper, a lawyer for Mr. Spitze, said in an email on Saturday that his client was a member of these groups because it was the only place where he could find validation and support he could not get from his parents.

Mr. Spitze, of Friendsville, Tenn., was not a part of these organizations because of their ideologies or dark principles, Mr. Cooper said.

He objected to “every single” accusation filed by the government, according to court papers filed by Mr. Cooper.

“The government portrayed Kyle as a demon, and many will call him a monster,” Mr. Cooper said. “However, it is the unfortunate truth that this young man is a product of his environment and our society.”

Mr. Spitze was part of online networks that relied on threats, blackmail and manipulation to get victims to produce or livestream self-harm and graphic content, prosecutors said.

The authorities identified at least 30 victims from around the world. One was 12 years old, according to court records.

Two victims, whose ages were not made public, died by suicide, the authorities said. One victim fled her country and changed her name to heal and feel safe, prosecutors said.

“The defendant’s criminal acts are a new breed of violence, so powerful the only tools the defendant needed were his phone and the internet,” prosecutors said in court documents. “During interviews with the F.B.I., the defendant’s victims outlined how the defendant was able to permanently scar victims across the world, physically and mentally, without ever having to lay a hand on them in person.”

The case began in December 2023, when the F.B.I. looked into tips that Harm Nation members had child sexual abuse imagery.

Discord, an online messaging platform, provided investigators with a report flagging members partaking in “high-harm activities,” prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze was among those flagged.

Investigators found he had pictures of young girls who cut themselves. The girls had written “Crim” or “Criminal” on their bodies with their own blood, which was a moniker Mr. Spitze used, prosecutors said.

Investigators searched Mr. Spitze’s cellphone after obtaining a search warrant in February 2024. They found similar images and videos, prosecutors said.

“The forensic examination of the defendant’s phone revealed the defendant had no legitimate employment, and spent countless hours finding, grooming and threatening victims,” prosecutors said.

One victim, a 12-year-old girl, began a casual and friendly conversation online with Mr. Spitze, prosecutors said.

Within three days, Mr. Spitze asked the girl to take nude photos of herself and sent her a graphic video. The girl also sent Mr. Spitze graphic footage of herself, prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze threatened to release those images if the victim did not meet his demands. She was also forced to kill a chicken and spell “crim” with its intestines, prosecutors said.

“Like a spider spinning a web, the defendant waited patiently, grooming his victims until he had them trapped,” prosecutors said. “The defendant then flooded his victim’s world with nonstop texting, direct messaging, video calls and demands for graphic content.”

Mr. Spitze pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child sexual exploitation material, one count of abetting the distribution of animal-crushing videos and possessing and accessing child exploitation material with an intent to view it, prosecutors said.

Mr. Spitze regretted his actions, Mr. Cooper said, and experienced mental health issues and abused substances from an early age. By pleading guilty, Mr. Spitze sought to avoid a prolonged trial and spare his victims further trauma, he added.

item.title: Officials Investigating Mail Carrier in Peacock Assault
item.description:
Officials said they are investigating a mail carrier after video surfaced of him appearing to strike a beloved peacock on Tuesday in a Pasadena, Calif., neighborhood.

Gina Davis, a member of the community, said her husband called her after finding the peacock, known as Sugar, in the street.

Ms. Davis said that she found Sugar with a swollen eye and that he could not move one of his wings.

She said she had checked footage from a security camera that had a view of the street, a corner of her house and a neighbor’s house.

In the video, posted by the television station ABC11, the peacock appears to be on the opposite side of a fence from the mail carrier. The carrier then appears to spray some kind of liquid in the direction of the bird.

Moments later, the carrier, who was not identified, appears to hurl something toward the peacock, the video shows. Another part of the video shows the peacock directly in front of the mail delivery truck, before the carrier strikes it with an object.

Sugar then topples over before collapsing.

According to Ms. Davis, the man in the video is the regular postal worker in the neighborhood. She said Sugar followed him “a lot” while he delivered mail.

“Postal employees in this area have experienced previous encounters with peacocks, and the Postal Service has been working with Pasadena Humane regarding concerns involving the birds,” the U.S. Postal Service said in a statement.

The Postal Service said it was reviewing what happened “and gathering the facts.”

“We expect our employees to conduct themselves professionally and appropriately while performing their duties,” it said.

Flocks of wild peacocks are common in the area, and Sugar is no stranger to the neighborhood.

Ms. Davis said she lived in the neighborhood for 25 years and Sugar was around for at least four of them. There were a number of peacocks around, but Sugar was the only white one.

“The peacocks are used to people,” she said. “They walk up to houses, lie in nests and bushes of the front yards.”

It’s not uncommon for neighbors to feed the peacocks, she said, adding that some keep fruit and seeds on hand as snacks for the birds. Sugar’s favorite treat is blackberries.

The treatment and condition of Sugar left Ms. Davis disheartened. On a typical day, Sugar wanders around the neighborhood, she said.

“He loves to scream and talk and is vocal, and he’s usually the loudest,” she said. “Like our neighborhood rooster,” she added.

In an interview on Saturday, Kevin McManus, a spokesman for Pasadena Humane, said that Sugar was being treated for his injuries and continues to heal.

Sugar was eating and “moving about normally, and the swelling around his injuries has gone down a bit,” he said.

“Our veterinarians and wildlife team will continue to monitor him, and the prognosis is positive that he will be able to released back to the wild,” Mr. McManus said.

Georgia Gee contributed research

item.title: Jackie O’s Private Beach Is Open to All. But It’s a Hike.
item.description:
Alex Wilcox Cheek’s alarm went off a few minutes before 10 a.m. on a recent Sunday to reserve a parking space at a trailhead on the farthest tip of Martha’s Vineyard. The pressure, he said, was not unlike buying coveted concerted tickets.

He would later spend a morning among the trees — oaks, beetlebungs, maples — gnarled with time and salt spray from the Atlantic Ocean. He wondered, Had anyone ever seen these trees up close, in person?

It was a fair question. After generations of private ownership, more than 330 acres in Aquinnah, once owned by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis and her daughter, Caroline Kennedy, opened to the public last year as the Squibnocket Pond Reservation, with a new trail added in July.

The property includes windswept moors, burbling creeks and an exclusive swimming beach. It not only offers a prime example of how one of history’s most famous families, back in the cultural discourse with shows like “Love Story” and a run at Congress, has enjoyed the privacy of natural beauty. But it also cracks open a corner of Martha’s Vineyard, so untouched, that other multimillion-dollar properties — and the affordable housing crisis created in their wake — don’t even seem to exist.

“There’s a serenity and a calm up here; it’s just been inaccessible in a lot of ways,” said Wilcox Cheek, who grew up coming to the area as a child.

But its inaccessibility, then and now, has worked in its favor.

“We’re really fortunate to have access to this corner of the island.”

In 1978, Onassis purchased the property, known as Red Gate Farm, for $1.1 million. Kennedy and her husband, Edwin Schlossberg, sold the land in 2020 for $27 million to two of the largest land conservation groups on the island, the Martha’s Vineyard Land Bank and the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation. (The property was once listed at $65 million.)

The reserve includes two separate holdings. The north entrance is a woodland walk, and the south entrance has multiple trails, including some that lead to a half-mile-long beach, and, new this summer, a trail that skirts along Squibnocket Pond. There, visitors can peer into an old hunting cabin where the former first lady once hosted lunches.

Next year, the land groups hope to make kayaks available to take onto the pond.

But getting there isn’t for the faint of heart. Parking spaces to access the south entrance are limited to 10 spots a day in the summer and require an online reservation. Cellphone service is sparse. Ticks are ever present. And it’s about a 25-minute walk down to the ocean.

“Our goal from the very outset was to sight the trailhead far away so that you had to walk to get there,” said James Lengyel, the executive director of the Land Bank. “And when you got there you would be rewarded by the remoteness and your ability to enjoy nature pretty much by yourself.”

In the late 1970s, Onassis told her children that “she had fallen in love with the rolling hills, wild dunes and silent ponds of Aquinnah,” Kennedy wrote in a letter to The Vineyard Gazette in 2019. “My mother believed that a North Atlantic summer was one of the most magical gifts in life.”

Red Gate Farm, named for the original gate that stood at the front of the property, “provided her with the sanctuary she needed and the freedom to be close to nature, her family, her friends and her books,” her daughter wrote. “It was a perfect expression of her romantic and adventurous spirit.”

Onassis was largely welcomed in town, both for her efforts in preserving the land and for keeping within the Vineyard way: biking to the Gay Head Lighthouse, paddling on her kayak, checking her lobster pots, grabbing ice cream with her grandchildren and keeping a low profile.

The bulk of the property’s sale took place in December 2020 for 304 acres for $27 million. A year later, the Land Bank bought an additional 32-acre lot from the family for $10 million. (Caroline Kennedy declined an interview for this story.)

The Kennedy-Schlossberg family kept the traditional Cape Cod-style house, guesthouse and surrounding 95 acres in the transaction. But if you’re hoping to get a glimpse of the Kennedy compound or run into Jack Schlossberg on the beach, you will be out of luck. The was preserve purposefully sited to maintain the family’s privacy.

Still, this land is steeped in Kennedy memories: John F. Kennedy Jr. could be seen windsurfing down on Squibnocket Pond in the 1990s, before he died in a plane crash not far from the family’s home. Tatiana Schlossberg, Caroline Kennedy’s daughter who died in January, was married at the family’s home in 2017. Many islanders can recall taking walks along the Atlantic beach, only to be turned around by an armed guard when the family was in residence.

Living year-round in a community where the economy relies largely on summer visitors has always been a difficult dance, none more so than in the last decade as soaring housing prices have trickled down to every facet of island life. But long before the concept of vacationland or a summer White House ever emerged, this land was — and remains — inhabited by the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah).

The Wampanoag have lived on the island, known as Noepe, for thousands of years, with a tribal community anchored in Aquinnah. The new reserve includes many sites like Black Brook and Witch Pond, which are rooted in Wampanoag mythology.

Tribal leaders said they were not contacted by the Kennedy-Schlossberg family ahead of the sale, and would have tried to find a way to bring the ancestral land back into their ownership or stewardship.

“Whether we purchase it or not, we should be considered,” Kevin Devine, the chairman of the tribe, said in an interview.

Tribal members do have special access rights to the land for sustenance purposes, including hunting and foraging.

“There has to be a balance between acknowledging the fact that we do have a housing crisis and we also have a development crisis,” said Tobias Vanderhoop, the secretary of the tribal council.

“The lands are sensitive. There has to be an eye toward acknowledging the fragility.”

“Every inch cannot be developed.”

In 2006, the Kennedy-Schlossberg family made a $100,000 donation to the town’s affordable housing committee as part of a new subdivision plan. For the Land Bank and Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation, that donation satisfied consideration of any further affordable housing needs on the property.

“When you look at the coast from Boston down to Washington, there’s very little that is natural,” Lengyel said. “So when you have an opportunity to protect something natural within those poles, you don’t trifle it away. You’ve gotta pay attention.”

But Juli Vanderhoop, the chairman of Aquinnah Board of Selectmen and a tribal member, said the affordable housing crisis facing the island, one that has forced many local families to move off-island, was too critical to ignore. Vanderhoop said she would have liked to see some of the property include housing, and for the tribe to have stewarded the land, as a way to support people who call Aquinnah home.

“What’s the responsibility of the conservation society to give back to the communities that hold these special places?” she said. “Really, I mean, because we’re losing them.”

Vanderhoop, who also owns Orange Peel Bakery in town, knows the magic of this corner of the island well.

“What has brought so much popularity to Aquinnah is the peace that this land brings to not just the people who live here, but the people who come back to our beaches, to this community, year after year after year,” she said. “It’s a peace that you can’t find any place in the entire world.”

Converting 336 acres of exclusive real estate into a nature preserve may not meet all of the island’s growing needs.

But the alternative — developing some of most ecologically diverse and sensitive land on Martha’s Vineyard — would have been far worse, tribal members said.

There are more than 30 rare species on the property, including spotted turtles, orchids and shorebirds. Adam Moore, the president of the Sheriff’s Meadow Foundation, admired one of the oak trees on a recent morning, and noted the different trunks sprouting from the stump.

“That’s one tree that was probably cut at one time,” he said. “That’s why it has one, two, three — no four — major trunks.”

Moore continued beyond the sea lavender and patches of poison ivy, crossing over raised boardwalks that zigzagged across windswept dunes. The ocean was at first a sliver on the horizon, and then unfurled without another person in sight.

Be careful of getting lost in the beauty on the boardwalks, he cautioned. “I’ve almost fallen off this because I start looking out,” he said.

A seal bobbed its head up to say hello, as terns skated across the water’s edge. The state of the beach is in the hands of the tides — sometimes it’s sandy, sometimes it’s rocky. But one thing is for sure, Moore said, “It’s a knockout beautiful beach.”

item.title: Two Phoenix Police Officers Fired and Arrested After Violent Traffic Stop
item.description:
Two Phoenix police officers, who were accused of beating a couple and shocking them with a stun gun during an unreported traffic stop this month, have been fired and arrested on charges including kidnapping, aggravated assault and aggravated robbery, the police chief said on Saturday.

The officers, Luis Vasquez Jr. and Antonio Felix, were on duty when they stopped the couple at about 11:30 p.m. on Aug. 5 in south Phoenix, Chief Matthew Giordano said at a news conference. Detectives have confirmed that the officers physically assaulted both the man and the woman, and the investigation showed that a Taser was used on them, he said.

Neither officer reported the stop or activated his body camera, and there is no video of the encounter, Chief Giordano said. The police have not determined why the officers stopped the couple or what motivated their actions, and there is no indication that they previously knew one another.

The episode was so unusual that the police in Tempe, Ariz., who learned of it after finding the couple’s abandoned car, initially suspected that the men might have been impersonating police officers.

“When I was first made aware of the situation, I had the same reaction,” Chief Giordano said. “There’s no way this could be Phoenix police officers. It’s so far outside the bounds of our policies.”

The Tempe police report describes a harrowing and violent encounter.

The man told the Tempe police that he and his girlfriend were parked in his mother’s Dodge Charger when they noticed a police S.U.V. nearby. After they drove off, the S.U.V. followed and pulled them over.

Two officers got out of the S.U.V., tried to open the Dodge’s doors and threatened to smash the driver’s-side window, the man told the Tempe police.

The couple repeatedly asked why they had been stopped, according to the police report. One officer reached into the car and unlocked the driver’s door as the other put the woman in an “arm bar” and threatened to break her arm if her boyfriend did not get out, and then shocked her in the thigh and back with a Taser, the report says.

After the woman was handcuffed and placed in the S.U.V., the man said the officers shocked him with a Taser, punched him repeatedly in the head and pulled his hair. One officer drew a gun and threatened to shoot him while counting down from three, prompting him to get out of the car, according to the report.

The man then jumped back into the car and sped away alone, leaving the woman with the officers, despite threats that he would be shot, according to the report. He said the car later overheated and he abandoned it in Tempe. The officers removed the woman’s handcuffs, told her, “We know where you live now,” and drove away, leaving her to walk home, according to the report.

The Tempe police found the Dodge the next day with a broken window and tires that smelled of burned rubber.

Chief Giordano thanked the Tempe police for finding the abandoned car and bringing the case to his department’s attention. He said the department had also begun a broader review to determine whether anyone else was involved and whether there were systemic problems.

There was no indication that other officers knew about the encounter, and no other officers had been placed on leave, Chief Giordano said. He also said that Mr. Vasquez and Mr. Felix had previous policy violations, though none were “of this nature.”

The former officers also face charges of felony assault involving a bound and otherwise physically restrained individual, threatening and intimidating, criminal damage, hindering prosecution and tampering with evidence.

item.title: Many Nashville Bus Stops Lack Places to Sit. These Locals Took a Stand.
item.description:
The first bench downtown was modest, just sanded wood with no paint. It was stamped with the words, “TO NASHVILLE WITH LOVE.” The next few were splashier, with bright colors and designs.

Now, at least 100 handmade benches have appeared at bus stops and elsewhere around the city, providing a place for riders to sit and wait.

But the benches, built by a band of civic-minded residents to fill a need they saw the city as neglecting, have become a flashpoint in the debate over whether Nashville is spending enough on its own residents as tourism becomes an ever-larger focus.

The city keeps removing benches, citing complaints and accusing the volunteer group of violating traffic laws with their placement. City officials say they are addressing the lack of benches — and could legalize those made by the group — but bureaucracy is slow.

“A lot of people use them — and also they just make the city prettier,” said Ivie Tran, 18. “What’s the problem with having your community sit down?”

Other American cities have removed benches to deter homeless people from loitering or sleeping. Indeed, the first handmade bench to appear in Nashville last summer served as a rebuke to the city after it had removed metal benches from a prominent downtown boulevard.

In a statement last year, the bench builders called seating at bus stops an “issue of basic human dignity,” and their efforts “a nonviolent protest against a city that insists upon hostile design.”

But as the effort expanded, it also became a grass-roots way of addressing the demand for public transit in Nashville. Higher gas prices helped increase ridership by 20 percent over three months.

A voter-approved program has slowly funded new shelters, benches and other transit changes — about 350 of the nearly 1,600 bus stops now include shelters, up from about 100 a decade ago. But many stops still lack seating or even a sidewalk.

The volunteer group has helped build and place benches over the last year, using donations and bulk purchases of wood. Ben Hubert, 31, a chemist, helped design a bench blueprint as “simple as humanly possible” for people new to the bench cause, he said.

“We can’t stand to see people standing on the side of the road,” he said. “We’ll do this for as long as people are willing to help chip in.”

Nashville officials are not, they say, opposed to providing places for riders to wait. But the city has removed some benches, arguing they were improperly placed. (The group denies this.)

Mayor Freddie O’Connell, a Democrat, said the city is merely trying to avoid liability.

An issue “tough for our legal department to swallow,” he said, “is who accepts the liability if something goes wrong.”

He noted the city has received complaints — especially, organizers have said, regarding benches painted with the phone number of a group that documents immigration enforcement. (He acknowledged that he found the benches in his neighborhood lovely.)

In a statement, Nashville’s Department of Transportation said that officials were working toward formally permitting the benches.

Some organizers are familiar and vocal critics of policing and other policies. They have bristled over what they say is a lack of funding for Nashville neighborhoods while taxpayer dollars go toward a new football stadium and business development, more evidence, they say, that tourists take priority over residents.

A bench, “is a symbol about a humane city,” said the Rev. Robin Lovett-Owen, 33, who helped place the first one. She added, “as a symbol, it’s immediately salient — it’s legible to people that people should be able to sit down.”

But as word has spread about the project, it has increasingly drawn people for reasons that have less to do with protest or activism.

“It’s been a sort of great conversation starter about community and how we can take care of others,” said Sharon Whitmore, 43, who had noticed the benches while driving.

Griffin Pacey, 27, drove to a recent Saturday morning bench-building event from nearby Hermitage with his partner. It was, Mr. Pacey said, a matter of “just looking for more ways to be involved in our communities. And we both love building things.”

With the bars and pedal taverns of downtown Nashville as a backdrop, organizers lined up two rows of completed benches for display on a recent steamy weekend. It was part of an event — sponsored in part by the Nashville Department of Transportation — where the group marked a year since they had started appearing.

The winning bench, it was decided, belonged to Ms. Whitmore, her husband and her two sons, Max and Teddy. It was blue, with silhouettes of animals and the capitalized words, “MIGRATION IS AN EARTH RIGHT.”

It was time to move the benches to nearby streets. One by one, they were loaded onto cargo bikes or into a pedicab covered in pink feathers.

It was unclear, the organizers acknowledged, how long they would stay put. At least for now, they said, people waiting for the bus could take a seat.

Lately, Nashville's been asking itself: Who is this city for? Watching these benches pop up around town felt like a fresh way to answer that. What stood out to me most, though, was just how eager people were to hang out and actually connect with their neighbors.

item.title: Angry Ohio Voters Could Turn Their State Purple Again
item.description:
Across Ohio, a state that receded from the nation’s political battle zone as its voting patterns turned an ever deeper shade of red, signs of discontent this year are everywhere.

In packed public forums, residents rage about data center projects. In grocery store aisles, shoppers lament to cashiers how little they can get for $50. In the soybean and corn fields, farmers express anxiety and pessimism. The basics of life and business have gotten punishingly expensive, and many have come to doubt that relief is coming anytime soon.

“It’s all dumpy. Businesses are closing, the roads look like crap,” Kim Hall, 59, said as she shopped at a Dollar General in North Ridgeville, Ohio, on Wednesday. “Grocery prices are outrageous, and I can barely afford to live.”

Frustration like hers is evident in every region and demographic in the state, and it’s why Ohio may be up for grabs in the 2026 midterms. With the general election less than 75 days away, polls show dead heats for governor and a coveted Senate seat. Enough congressional seats are in play for either party to swing control of the House. Come November, the state that once bragged “So goes Ohio, so goes the nation” will find out if it is truly inching back toward purple.

But how voter frustrations will play out is anyone’s guess. Ms. Hall, who worked as a cook at McDonald’s until a kidney cancer diagnosis last year, was once an enthusiast for President Trump. In 2024, she voted for Kamala Harris. This fall, she said she is likely to give up on voting.

“I don’t like anybody,” she said. “I don’t agree with any of them.”

Nan Whaley, a former mayor of Dayton who ran for governor in 2022, said she believes that Ohio Democrats are landing with their message: “You hate everything and you can’t be mad at the Democrats. They haven’t been in control.”

She is reluctant to make predictions, having seen Democrats in Ohio get burned by false hope before, but the vibe is clear.

“People are just so — I’ve just not seen them this pissed,” she said.

On this, even the state’s Republicans agree. Jim Renacci, a former congressman who also ran for governor in 2022, has been flooding his Facebook page with dire warnings to his fellow conservatives. Ohio, he said in an interview, is at heart a state of independents who lean conservative, but those people must be won over at a time when they have a multitude of reasons to stay home from the polls.

“You can get mad at me for posting this. But I am just delivering the message,” he wrote to his followers this month, adding: “The biggest issues for Independents are: Iran War. Gas prices. Food prices. Utility bills. Rent.”

In rural Mercer County on the state’s western border, that list also includes the costs of fertilizer and farm machinery, which were increased by the Iran conflict and the global trade war. Few in the deeply conservative area are inclined to blame the president. But some of the farmers who were loading cattle at the Mercer County fair allowed that business conditions were getting scary, and that was before Mr. Trump announced on Friday that he planned to lower tariffs on foreign beef imports.

Diane Sheets, 77, who splits a 160-acre soybean farm with her sister and works at a travel plaza to make ends meet, said that politicians just don’t seem interested in people’s economic troubles.

“They might understand, but I don’t think they care,” she said. “Do you see them trying to help us any time?”

This same sense of powerlessness is fueling the fury over data centers.

In Millersport, a village outside Columbus, a school cafeteria was packed for a hearing last week about a proposed power plant that would provide energy to a $2.1 billion data center project being built in nearby farmland. The residents in the cafeteria were virtually unanimous in opposition: A Democratic statehouse candidate wearing a Pride pin railed against the process, her criticisms later echoed by an Air Force veteran wearing a “Don’t Tread on Me” shirt with an Infowars logo.

It’s not just in Millersport. Those packing into meeting halls across the state express detailed objections about the ramifications for local waterways, the unfairness of tax breaks and the effects of pollution on children who live nearby. But their protests tap into a deeper conviction — that outsiders are making decisions about their communities without their consent.

“The way things look, it’s hard to have hope for anything, honestly,” said Wayne Harris, 68, whose anger was kindled by a planned 1,550-acre solar farm near Millersport, and burned hotter with the coming of the data center.

In both cases, he said, he learned about a major project in his community only after it was too late to do much about it. Both projects would “ruin” the quiet rural life the local residents had known, he said. He has written letters to the president on down, but he does not expect anyone to step in given the power of the corporations behind the projects.

“They have all the attorneys and all the money,” he said. “They just kind of laugh in your face at you, like, ‘We can do what we want.’”

Mr. Harris blamed the Biden administration for the solar farm and said he did not trust Amy Acton, the Democrat running for Ohio governor. But the backlash to data centers across the state has become so widespread that Republican campaign officials are nervous.

In a recent memo sent to tech companies, first reported by Axios, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned that Democrats were harnessing the backlash to data centers in the Ohio Senate race, and that they were doing it “because it works.”

In campaign ads, former Senator Sherrod Brown, a Democrat angling for a comeback, has labeled the Republican incumbent, Senator Jon Husted, as “the face of data centers in Ohio.” Ads for Mr. Husted, meantime, have disparaged Mr. Brown’s previous long reign in the Senate, saying “Sherrod Brown is Washington.”

“More than any other thing in this race,” the Republican memo read, “data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

If the Senate race has Washington’s attention, the governor’s race embodies many of Ohioans’ frustrations. The Republican nominee, Vivek Ramaswamy, captures one element of voter rage: He’s a billionaire who made his mint off pharmaceuticals, finance and technology. But the Democrat, Dr. Acton, carries her own baggage in an environment where trust is in short supply: She guided state Covid policy in the opening months of the pandemic.

While Dr. Acton is fighting the state’s rightward lean, Mr. Ramaswamy is facing a more acute problem: representing the party in power before a broadly unhappy electorate. In a June New York Times/Siena poll of likely voters in Ohio, nearly 30 percent of voters, and 40 percent of independents, said the economy or cost of living was the most important issue in deciding their vote for Congress. In that same poll, people disapproved of Mr. Trump’s handling of the cost of living by a nearly 2-to-1 margin.

Some Republicans say Democratic optimism is misplaced. Years of infrastructure building and G.O.P. control in the state, they say, has given their party a firewall.

“Those built-up grass roots advantages are hard to overcome in one outlier cycle,” said Mark R. Weaver, a Republican consultant and former Ohio deputy attorney general.

In reliably blue Summit County at the cafe of a locally owned health foods store, a group of liberal voters spent hours hand writing postcards to voters, all with the same message, designed to tap into the rage of the moment.

“Dear Eric, While working families struggle, billionaires and MAGA politicians are cashing in,” they wrote over and over, before advocating that Eric — or Heather or Barbara or all the other names on their precisely targeted list — come out and vote for Mr. Brown.

Bill Jordan, a suspenders-wearing retired law professor who has organized postcard-writing events since 2020, used to instruct his companions to write to people in states like Georgia or Virginia, where races felt more winnable. This year, Mr. Jordan, 76, has his hopes up for Ohio. His list was designed to drum up turnout from young people and voters who had cast their ballots for Democrats in the past but typically skipped the midterms.

Taylor Dupont, a 30-year-old software engineer, fell into both categories. Lorain County, where she lives, west of Cleveland, is the only Ohio county that went for both Mr. Trump and Mr. Brown in 2024. Her employer recently told her and around 200 of her co-workers that their jobs were being eliminated. Her child’s school district then cut busing, meaning she’d have to put more miles on her beat-up Kia at a time when gas prices felt outrageous.

Her grocery costs, utility bills and rent on her two-bedroom duplex were all rising, and she didn’t know what to do about it all. But she did know who she blamed: “The president,” she said, “and the billionaires.”

On Wednesday, she was combing through the half-off aisle at Goodwill. She said she planned to vote in the midterms for the first time, straight Democratic, but she hadn’t yet paid too much attention to any of the races. She needed to land another job, get her car fixed, and before any of that, find her daughter outfits for her first week of school.

“Remember,” she told her soon-to-be fifth grader, “we are looking for needs, not wants.”

item.title: This Canal System Transformed Arizona. It’s Now in Jeopardy.
item.description:
From a secure, windowless room in northern Phoenix, technicians control the Colorado River water that sustains America’s largest desert metropolis.

The vast canal system the team oversees has for four decades conveyed an increasingly scarce commodity across 330 miles of rugged terrain to slake blossoming subdivisions, sprawling farmland and, in recent years, a powerhouse semiconductor industry. It supercharged Arizona’s economy and transformed Phoenix into one of the nation’s fastest-growing cities.

But this lifeline, known as the Central Arizona Project, came with a catch. In exchange for billions of federal dollars to build it, the state agreed to lower-priority water rights, putting the aqueduct among the first in line for cuts in a time of deep drought.

Now that time has come.

“It was the price we had to pay,” said Kathryn Sorensen, a former water director for the city of Phoenix. “The chickens have come home to roost.”

With the seven states that rely on the Colorado River deadlocked over how to split its diminishing supply, the Trump administration is pushing its own plan to divide the water. The three downriver states — Arizona, California and Nevada — would most likely shoulder the most pain, but no single user stands to lose more than the Central Arizona Project.

Short-term reductions, announced by the federal government on Friday, will cost Arizona roughly one-third of its share of river water over the next two years. But beyond that, a range of cutbacks remain possible.

Under the most severe outcome, the system would be cut off entirely during the driest years, setting off a social and economic meltdown Arizonans shudder to even imagine.

“They are threatening to shut down the Southwest,” said Brenda Burman, the project’s general manager. “It’s not possible to picture it.”

Water is gold in the western United States, and people have been fighting over every drop for generations. The Colorado, a river that supports 40 million residents and is buckling after decades of drought and overuse, is the fiercest battleground of all. Access to it is governed by an arcane legal system that prioritizes the oldest established users.

The earliest laws were written for a river that no longer exists, and states do not agree on how to proceed. The high-stakes talks have gained urgency as the water levels of the river’s largest two reservoirs, Lakes Mead and Powell, have dwindled in recent weeks to record lows.

Arizona officials say any proposal that cuts off the state’s canal system is unacceptable, and they have threatened to sue, initiating court battles that could go on for years. For now, water experts say, taps and sprinklers will continue running from Phoenix to Tucson.

But any serious hit to the state’s Colorado River supply is likely to drive up the cost of replacement water and lead to more groundwater pumping, jeopardizing an already depleted safety net for future generations.

Human life in the parched Southwest has always depended on harnessing water.

The prehistoric Hohokam people built a flourishing society in the Sonoran Desert by carving a network of irrigation canals. Hundreds of years after the mysterious disappearance of the canals, the Bureau of Reclamation in 1911 dedicated its first major dam outside Phoenix to bring more settlers to the valley.

But state leaders knew they would need another source of water to continue growing, and they had their eyes on the Colorado River.

“The Central Arizona Project was Arizona’s holy grail,” said Thomas E. Sheridan, a historian who has written extensively about the system’s origins.

After decades of bitter interstate disputes, Congress approved construction of the aqueduct in 1968. The project would suck water from the Colorado and transport it to faraway cities, tribes and farms — an engineering marvel and a testament to the country’s belief that it could bend nature to its will.

But California cajoled Arizona into a compromise. Even during times of shortage, the Golden State would get its full allocation of water, no matter what.

When the project made its first deliveries to Phoenix in 1985, the celebration was tempered by foreboding: “The time is going to come in the not too distant future when we are going to be looking for water again,” a congressman cautioned at the time.

Cities that count on the Central Arizona Project have tried to prepare. The region now uses less water than it did 40 years ago, even as its population has more than doubled, and it has frantically recharged its aquifers.

Most Arizona officials do not expect the federal government to approve more massive water infrastructure projects, but they insist Congress should help pay for smaller-scale solutions like desalination plants or dam expansions.

In Phoenix, which gets about 40 percent of its water from the canal, Mayor Kate Gallego said the federal government should kick in more for multibillion dollar purification plants that will turn wastewater into drinking water. She compared such funding with aid that helps coastal states rebuild after hurricanes — a national response to a different type of disaster.

“Given the magnitudes of these cuts, we would like them to step up in a really big and meaningful way,” Ms. Gallego said.

Cave Creek, a picturesque burg steeped in cowboy kitsch in the foothills north of Phoenix, gets 95 percent of its water from the aqueduct system.

“Without Colorado River water, we would be a dusty little town with dirt roads,” Mayor Robert Morris said.

The town’s leaders have been scrambling to find backup plans. Cave Creek has hired a water consultant and struck deals with neighboring municipalities, cobbling together enough supply for the next five years, Mr. Morris said.

He has sought to prepare residents for higher bills and stricter conservation, working to undo a foundational part of the state’s philosophy in the process.

“The biggest thing for people to overcome is the idea of unlimited, cheap water,” Mr. Morris said.

In 2022, the canal project cut off most of its deliveries to the region’s nontribal agricultural fields, which have lower priority rights than cities. Those reductions would continue under the proposed federal framework.

Even tribes, which hold the most senior water rights in the state, are concerned about the federal government’s doomsday situation.

Members of the Ak-Chin Indian Community, who use Colorado River water to grow barley, potatoes and corn on 16,000 acres south of Phoenix, are not sure how that water would be delivered if the Central Arizona Project lost its entire allotment.

The uncertainty has reopened old wounds. In the 1970s, after failing to prevent nontribal farmers from draining an aquifer below the Ak-Chin reservation, Congress passed a law to ensure the tribe would always have an alternative source.

“It’s deeply concerning if this promise to us will once again be broken,” said Gabriel Lopez, the tribe’s chairman.

The tribe, whose name refers to traditional irrigation methods, has tried to conserve, Mr. Lopez added, and its farms now mostly use more efficient sprinkler systems.

“We always say ‘water is life,’ and that can’t be more true than it is today,” he said.

State leaders have urged the Trump administration to reconsider its planned cuts, which they say are built on faulty legal grounds and a misunderstanding of Arizona’s water rights.

Under the current plan, upper-basin states — Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Wyoming — do not face mandatory cutbacks. Tom Buschatzke, Arizona’s lead Colorado River negotiator, has pushed the federal government to spread the pain more evenly.

In a pointed letter to federal officials this month, Mr. Buschatzke argued that the administration’s proposal flouted the Colorado River Compact, the 1922 agreement that divvied up the waterway.

“These are draconian outcomes for Arizona,” he said in an interview.

At the Central Arizona Project’s headquarters, water dispatchers, who pull marathon shifts in the command center, are preparing to work with channels that are less full.

As the air conditioning hummed and a map displayed live readings of water flows across central Arizona on a recent morning, the technicians could feel the weight of their responsibility.

“We can’t afford to be making mistakes,” said Andrew Tatlow, a water control supervisor. “Every drop of water counts.”

item.title: The Midterms Feel Like 2006 All Over Again
item.description:
The war in the Middle East is increasingly unpopular. So is the president as his numbers dip perilously — a common development in the sixth year of a presidency. Congressional Republicans are embroiled in unsavory scandals. Americans are shelling out big bucks for gas while economic anxiety runs high.

The grim backdrop for November’s midterm elections has created a steep challenge for Republicans and opportunities for Democrats that look much the same as those they encountered in 2006. Back then, congressional Republicans faced the voters at the midpoint of President George W. Bush’s second term, with the public roiled by the war in Iraq, high fuel prices and a series of ugly accusations against members of the G.O.P. majority on Capitol Hill.

“It is striking,” said Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic minority leader and chief architect of his party’s Senate campaign strategy this year and two decades ago. “The analogy is amazing.”

The parallels are not perfect, since politics and campaigns have both changed radically over 20 years. But the comparisons are instructive, as officials in both parties stare down the final months of an election that will determine who controls Congress for the remainder of President Trump’s term.

“This is 2006 2.0,” said Rahm Emanuel, who in 2006 was an ambitious Democratic House member from Illinois and Mr. Schumer’s counterpart across the Capitol as the head of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee. “The similarities are eerie.”

Mr. Emanuel and Mr. Schumer both have good reason to look back fondly on 2006, when Democrats triumphed in a blue wave.

Exceeding expectations that year, Democrats picked up six seats in the Senate, taking control of the chamber. In the House, where the Republican majority seemed to have exhausted itself after a dozen years, Democrats gained 31 seats and installed Nancy Pelosi, who is now retiring, as the first woman speaker. Mr. Bush, another victim of the six-year presidential itch, famously branded the outcome “a thumping.”

This year, the Senate map is stacked against Democrats — they would need to win at least four Republican-held seats to take control, all but one of them in states that Mr. Trump won in 2024. And not all of the most competitive races have gone as party leaders had hoped. But Democrats have benefited from some political twists in places where they had not anticipated being competitive, such as in Texas, where Mr. Trump’s primary endorsement of the state’s attorney general, Ken Paxton, over Senator John Cornyn, put that seat in play.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report on Thursday moved its ratings of the Texas and Iowa Senate races from leaning Republican to a toss up, underscoring the expanding battleground that Democrats would need in order to replicate 2006. Democrats say that they believe they are also increasingly competitive in other states carried by Mr. Trump two years ago, including Kansas.

While clear similarities exist this year, significant differences are present as well — not the least of which is that Americans consume and process political content far differently than they did 20 years ago, with an emphasis on digital media rather than traditional television advertising.

Other structural changes have taken place that could influence the results. The two parties this year engaged in a redistricting war that could help stem some of the House losses Republicans might have suffered in a midterm year that traditionally runs against those in power. Polarization runs deeper, making it harder to shake voters from their party identification. Mr. Trump’s hold on his base seems stronger than Mr. Bush’s was in 2006, though it is potentially weakening amid a backlash to the war with Iran.

In the Senate and the House, the Democratic establishment did not get its preferred candidates through the primaries in some key races, including in Maine and Michigan. And the rise of far-left socialist candidates has Republicans seeing an opening to try to brand Democratic contenders across the country as part of a movement out of step with typical Americans.

For those reasons and more, Republicans say the comparison between the two elections comes up short.

“Democrats are running with a radically different party on a dramatically different map, and the fundamentals are stacked against them,” Mike Marinella, a spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement. “Republicans have stronger candidates, a historic fund-raising advantage and a more favorable battlefield, while Democrats are letting socialists hijack must-win races from Michigan to Colorado, Arizona, California and Maine.”

In 2006, the war with Iraq was the central issue in the campaign as Americans soured on Mr. Bush’s handling of the conflict, particularly after his main justification for the invasion — the claim that Saddam Hussein had weapons of mass destruction — turned out to be false. Mr. Trump’s conflict with Iran has not gone on nearly as long, nor has it produced the same level of casualties. But Mr. Bush had significantly more support at the start. Public opposition helped drive approval numbers for the two presidents below 40 percent, a dangerous midterm level, as both wars also drove up fuel costs.

Then as now, Democrats tried to capitalize on kitchen-table economic concerns with the potential to drive voters. In 2006, it was Mr. Bush’s proposal to privatize Social Security, which never came to pass. Now, it is the Republican-written law slashing Medicaid and other safety net programs to pay for large tax cuts, as well as the G.O.P.’s decision to allow health care subsidies to expire, sending premiums soaring.

“We found an issue early,” Mr. Schumer said, recalling 2006. “Rahm and I did Social Security. Now we found the costs issue, particularly led by health care.”

Another undercurrent of the 2006 campaign has an equivalent today: the image of disturbing Republican misconduct. Twenty years ago, Democrats campaigned against a “culture of corruption,” pointing to a series of financial and sex scandals that led to resignations and jail time for a series of senior Republicans.

Then, in September 2006, it was disclosed that Representative Mark Foley, Republican of Florida, had sent sexually suggestive messages to male House pages, and that Republican leaders had failed to take action even when they had been alerted to his actions, putting a cloud over the party two months before the election.

This year, Republicans have again had to contend with high-profile sexual misconduct accusations against multiple House members, though Democrats have had their own to deal with as well, a difference from 20 years ago.

Top Democrats have sought to emphasize Republican conduct on Capitol Hill and in an administration in which the president, his family and his allies have faced scrutiny for profiteering. In an appearance on NBC’s “Meet the Press” earlier this month, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader, said a central element of the Democratic campaign agenda was “pushing back against the corruption that has been unleashed on the American people, and holding the crooks accountable beginning on day one in January of next year.”

It is not clear whether it will all add up to a repeat of 2006. But Nathan Gonzales, the editor of the nonpartisan Inside Elections, sees the potential for the factors working against Republicans building into a resounding voter backlash against the party in power, as they did two decades ago.

“I remember 2006 when everything snowballed against Republicans,” Mr. Gonzales said. “Ordinarily unrelated events got lumped together under one umbrella. Everything was Bush’s fault. The war with Iraq and Mark Foley really had nothing to do with each other, but it cultivated an appetite for change. I could see that happening again.”
